passages.happening:
‘Again I looked, and I considered all the oppression taking place under the sun’ (verse 1). The Teacher saw ‘the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter’ (verse 1).

‘So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive’ (verse 2). ‘But better than both is he who has not yet existed, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with the Teacher seeing injustice in the courts and trusting that God will judge. Chapter 4 looks at injustice more closely and more painfully, from the side of those who suffer it.

In the ancient world, people without family or patrons had no one to defend them. A comforter was someone who stood beside a person in grief or distress, usually family or friends. The Teacher says it twice in one verse: no comforter. The oppressed were truly alone.

Oppression by the powerful was a constant reality, under Israel's own kings, whom the prophets condemned for exploiting the poor, and under the empires that came after. The Teacher's words are not tied to any one ruler.
passages.later: Lamentations uses the same words for Jerusalem in ruins: ‘Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her’ (Lamentations 1:2). And Job, in his grief, cried something like verse 3: ‘Why did I not perish at birth’ (Job 3:11), he asked.
passages.hard:
Is it right to say that the dead, or those never born, are better off than the living?

Verses 2 and 3 say the Teacher admired the dead above the living, and counted better than both the one who has never been born and so has not seen the evil done under the sun. These are among the darkest words in Scripture.

Some readers take them as a settled view. Others read them as the Teacher's cry at seeing overwhelming injustice, the kind of cry also heard in Job 3 and Jeremiah 20, where suffering men curse the day they were born. The Bible includes such cries without making them its final truth. They are honest words of anguish, kept as part of God's word.

The book does not stay here. Later it says that ‘even a live dog is better than a dead lion’ (9:4), and again and again it commends life's goods as gifts from God. A reader facing their own darkness can find in these verses company, not a verdict. Scripture knows how dark life can look, and makes room for that honesty. It does not say that anyone is better off dead.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The oppressed had no comforter. Ask whose tears you have seen and passed by. And ask whether there is one person you could stand beside this week, so that they are not alone.

passages.t: Envy, one quiet handful, and two better than one
passages.happening:
‘I saw that all labor and success spring from a man’s envy of his neighbor. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 4). ‘The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh’ (verse 5). ‘Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind’ (verse 6).

Then a man alone, with no son or brother. There is no end to his work, and his eyes are never content with his wealth. He never stops to ask whom he is working for and why he denies himself every good thing (verse 8).

‘Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor’ (verse 9). “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!” (verse 10). Two who lie down together keep warm (verse 11). ‘And though one may be overpowered, two can resist. Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Verse 4 is a sharp diagnosis: much hard work is driven by comparison, by wanting what the neighbor has.

Verses 5 and 6 set two sayings side by side. The fool folds his hands and starves. Yet one handful with quiet is better than two with toil. Together they chart a middle course between laziness and driven overwork.

A man with no son or brother had no heir to carry his name or receive his property, and no one to care for him in old age. The man of verse 8 works anyway, endlessly, and never enjoys any of it.

Verses 9 to 12 make their case with three examples: falling, keeping warm, and defense against attack. Two people sharing a single cloak on a cold night was a practical need for travelers and the poor. Ropes were made by twisting strands together for strength, and the count climbs from two to three. Many readers apply the cord to marriage or friendship, though the text itself makes a general point about companionship.
passages.later: The Bible's first word about people says the same: ‘It is not good for the man to be alone’ (Genesis 2:18). And Paul asks believers to do what verse 10 describes: ‘Carry one another’s burdens’ (Galatians 6:2).
passages.asks: Two are better than one. Ask who would lift you up if you fell, and whom you would lift. And ask whether envy is driving more of your work than you would like to admit.

passages.t: The wise youth and the forgotten king
passages.happening:
‘Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning’ (verse 13). The youth came out of prison to become king, though he was born poor (verse 14). Everyone followed him (verse 15).

But there is no end to the people, and those who come later will not celebrate him either. ‘This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This little story has prompted many guesses. Joseph went from prison to power in Egypt, and David replaced Saul, but no single figure fits every detail. The Hebrew of verses 14 to 16 is difficult, and it is not clear exactly who comes from prison or who the ‘second one’ is. Most interpreters read it as a parable, not a report of one event.

Its point is the fickleness of fame. A wise young ruler is better than a foolish old one. But the crowd that cheers the newcomer will forget him too.
passages.later: Joseph's story shows a rise like the one in verse 14: ‘So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon’ (Genesis 41:14).
passages.asks: Even the cheered newcomer is forgotten. Ask how much of your sense of worth rests on being noticed. And ask whether, like the old king, there is a warning you have stopped being willing to hear.
